questions.q: A 25-year-old farmer presents with a highly inflammatory, boggy, pustular mass on his scalp after working closely with cattle. KOH examination reveals fungal hyphae. Which ecological category of dermatophyte is most likely responsible, and what characteristic feature explains the intense inflammatory response?
opts: Anthropophilic; adapted to human host causing chronic infection
Zoophilic; humans are abnormal hosts triggering acute inflammation
Geophilic; soil saprophyte causing mild self-limiting infection
Anthropophilic; transmitted via fomites causing vesicular eruption
questions.exp: Zoophilic dermatophytes like T. verrucosum (associated with cattle) cause acute, intense inflammatory responses in humans because humans are abnormal hosts. This often manifests as kerion formation, vesicles, and pustules, and may be self-resolving.

questions.q: A 65-year-old diabetic patient presents with a chronic leg ulcer that has failed to heal despite 3 months of treatment. Wound culture reveals a bacterial load of 10^6 CFU/gram of tissue. Which of the following best explains the mechanism by which this bacterial burden impairs wound healing?
opts: Direct cytotoxic destruction of fibroblasts by bacterial endotoxins
Competition for oxygen and nutrients with release of proteases that degrade ECM and growth factors
Inhibition of keratinocyte stem cell differentiation
questions.exp: Bacteria compete with host cells for vital oxygen and nutrients and stimulate an excessive inflammatory response that releases proteases (e.g., MMPs and elastase), which degrade essential extracellular matrix components and growth factors. A bacterial load exceeding 10^5 CFU/gram significantly impedes healing.

questions.q: A 12-year-old boy with cervical lymph node tuberculosis on treatment develops asymptomatic grouped follicular papules on the trunk. Mantoux test is strongly positive. Which histological finding would be expected in this condition?
opts: Wedge-shaped dermal necrosis with leukocytoclastic vasculitis
Caseating granulomas with numerous acid-fast bacilli
questions.exp: Lichen scrofulosorum presents as grouped follicular and perifollicular lichenoid papules in children with underlying active TB focus, commonly lymphadenitis. The lesions show perifollicular granulomatous inflammation histologically, and like other tuberculids, AFB are characteristically absent.

questions.q: On electron microscopy of normal epidermis, desmosomes show a characteristic intercellular space containing a dense midline. What is the width of this intercellular space?
questions.exp: Desmosomes appear as symmetrical junctions with a characteristic 30-nm intercellular space containing a dense line on electron microscopy. This intercellular space was historically termed 'desmoglea' and represents the adhesive interface between cells.

questions.q: High-throughput genomic sequencing of Mycosis fungoides has revealed a prominent mutational signature associated with which of the following environmental factors?
questions.exp: Genomic sequencing studies have identified a prominent ultraviolet (UV) mutational signature in Mycosis fungoides, suggesting that UV radiation acts as a major mutagen before clonal expansion of the malignant T-cells occurs.

questions.q: Which of the following clinical scenarios best exemplifies the 'Persistent' criterion in the SPUR warning signs for primary immunodeficiency?
opts: Two episodes of bacterial meningitis in one year
Oral thrush persisting despite 4 weeks of appropriate antifungal therapy
Infection with Aspergillus fumigatus in a child
questions.exp: Persistent infections are those that fail to clear completely or respond slowly despite adequate appropriate antimicrobial therapy. Oral thrush not resolving after 4 weeks of treatment indicates a persistent infection, whereas the other options represent serious, recurrent, or unusual infections respectively.

questions.q: A neonate born to a mother with untreated syphilis shows hepatosplenomegaly and skeletal abnormalities. Histopathological examination of affected tissues would most characteristically reveal which finding?
opts: Granulomatous inflammation with Langhans giant cells
Obliterative endarteritis with plasma cell infiltration
questions.exp: Congenital syphilis, like acquired syphilis, is histologically characterized by obliterative endarteritis with mononuclear and plasma cell infiltration surrounding blood vessels, intimal hyperplasia, and swollen endothelial cells.

questions.q: A patient with a healing surgical wound develops poor wound strength and dehiscence. Clinical examination reveals perifollicular hemorrhages and corkscrew hairs. Which enzymatic process is most likely impaired in this patient?
opts: Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase-mediated collagen cross-linking
questions.exp: Vitamin C is an essential cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase, enzymes required for collagen cross-linking and stabilization. Deficiency leads to unstable collagen fibrils, poor wound strength, dehiscence, and characteristic findings like perifollicular hemorrhage and corkscrew hairs (scurvy).

questions.q: A 12-year-old girl is scheduled to receive the HPV vaccine as part of the national immunization program. Her mother asks about the mechanism by which the vaccine provides protection. Which of the following best describes the composition of HPV vaccines?
opts: Live attenuated viral particles with reduced virulence
Inactivated whole virus particles containing viral DNA
Virus-like particles composed of L1 capsid protein without viral DNA
Recombinant viral vectors expressing E6 and E7 oncoproteins
questions.exp: HPV vaccines contain Virus-Like Particles (VLPs) made from the L1 major capsid protein that self-assembles into empty viral capsids. These VLPs are morphologically identical to native HPV virions but contain no viral DNA, making them non-infectious while remaining highly immunogenic.

questions.q: A microbiologist examining a fungal culture from a patient with onychomycosis identifies macroconidia that are smooth-walled, thin, and club-shaped (beaver tail appearance), with complete absence of microconidia. Which dermatophyte genus does this morphology represent?
questions.exp: Epidermophyton is uniquely characterized by smooth, thin-to-thick-walled, club-shaped (beaver tail) macroconidia and the complete absence of microconidia. This genus infects skin and nails but does not invade hair.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with numerous symmetrical, vague, shiny skin lesions and bilateral thickened earlobes. Skin biopsy reveals dermis packed with foamy macrophages containing numerous acid-fast bacilli, separated from a flattened epidermis by a clear zone. The Mitsuda reaction is negative. What cytokine profile predominates in this patient's immune response to the infection?
opts: IL-4, IL-5, and IL-10 dominant (Th2 response)
questions.exp: This patient has polar lepromatous leprosy (LL), characterized by foamy macrophages (Virchow cells), high bacillary load, Grenz zone, and negative lepromin test. LL exhibits a Th2-biased cytokine profile with high IL-4, IL-5, and IL-10, which suppress macrophage activation and Th1 responses, allowing unchecked bacterial multiplication.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with a painful, bluish nodule on her upper back that has been present for 2 years. Histopathology reveals well-circumscribed basophilic nodules in the dermis composed of two cell types - peripheral small dark basaloid cells and central larger pale cells - with prominent lymphocytic infiltration. Which genetic mutation is most likely associated with this tumor when it occurs sporadically?
opts: ALPK1 missense mutation in the kinase domain
questions.exp: This clinical and histopathological description is characteristic of eccrine spiradenoma. In sporadic (non-syndromic) spiradenomas, a recurrent missense mutation in the kinase domain of the ALPK1 gene has been identified, which activates the NF-κB pathway and is mutually exclusive with CYLD mutations.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with an oval-shaped, ivory-white plaque on her trunk surrounded by a violaceous border. The lesion is indurated centrally with loss of hair follicles. Which stage of morphea does the violaceous border specifically indicate?
opts: Active inflammatory stage with ongoing disease
Burnt out stage with residual pigmentation
questions.exp: The lilac ring (violaceous border) surrounding the fibrotic portion of a morphea plaque is characteristic of the active inflammatory stage, indicating ongoing disease activity. This clinical sign helps differentiate active lesions requiring treatment from inactive, burnt-out lesions.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man undergoes cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen for a basal cell carcinoma on his nose. The dermatologist performs two freeze-thaw cycles. What is the primary mechanism responsible for tumor cell death in this procedure?
opts: Direct intracellular ice crystal formation causing immediate membrane rupture
Delayed vascular injury leading to ischemic necrosis
Osmotic lysis during the rapid freezing phase
questions.exp: While direct cellular injury from intracellular ice crystals occurs during rapid freezing, the major/primary mechanism of tumor cell death in cryotherapy is delayed vascular injury. This involves endothelial damage, platelet aggregation, microthrombus formation, and subsequent ischemic necrosis during the thawing phase.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with recurrent tender nodules on the posterior calves that have ulcerated over the past few months. She has a BMI of 32 and works as a cashier standing for long hours. Biopsy shows lobular panniculitis with granulomatous inflammation and vasculitis affecting medium-sized vessels. Mantoux test is strongly positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Erythema induratum of Bazin typically affects young-to-middle-aged women with venous stasis or obesity, presenting as tender subcutaneous nodules on posterior calves that frequently ulcerate. The characteristic histopathology shows lobular panniculitis with granulomatous inflammation and vasculitis affecting medium-sized vessels.

questions.q: A patient with Brooke-Spiegler syndrome develops multiple skin tumors. On histopathology, one tumor shows basophilic nodules with two cell populations and scattered lymphocytes, while another shows islands of cells surrounded by thick PAS-positive hyaline sheaths in a jigsaw pattern. What is the most accurate statement regarding these tumors?
opts: They arise from different embryological lineages and occur together coincidentally
They share a common progenitor and differentiate toward the secretory portion of sweat glands
The lymphocyte-rich tumor is of eccrine origin while the other is apocrine
They are caused by mutations in different genes on separate chromosomes
questions.exp: Spiradenomas and cylindromas share a morphologic spectrum and common progenitor, both differentiating toward the secretory portion of the sweat gland. In Brooke-Spiegler syndrome, both tumors arise due to CYLD gene mutations and can even merge to form hybrid spiradenocylindromas within the same lesion.

questions.q: A dermatologist treats multiple seborrheic keratoses on a dark-skinned patient with cryotherapy. Which cellular population's sensitivity explains why hypopigmentation is the most common complication, occurring even before scarring would develop?
opts: Keratinocytes with lethal temperature of -20°C to -40°C
Fibroblasts with lethal temperature of -30°C to -35°C
Melanocytes with lethal temperature of -4°C to -7°C
Langerhans cells with lethal temperature of -15°C to -20°C
questions.exp: Melanocytes are the most cryosensitive cells in the skin, undergoing cell death at just -4°C to -7°C. This extreme sensitivity explains why hypopigmentation commonly occurs after cryotherapy, even with brief or superficial treatments that would not damage the more resistant keratinocytes or fibroblasts.

questions.q: A 17-year-old immunocompetent male presents for HPV vaccination. According to CDC (ACIP) guidelines, what is the recommended vaccination schedule for this patient?
questions.exp: According to CDC/ACIP guidelines, individuals aged 15-26 years require a 3-dose series administered at 0, 1-2, and 6 months. The 2-dose schedule (0 and 6-12 months) is reserved for those initiating vaccination between ages 9-14 years.

questions.q: A 4-year-old child presents with recurrent pneumonia (5 episodes in 2 years), chronic otitis media requiring multiple courses of antibiotics, and a recent hospitalization for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. According to the SPUR criteria for suspecting primary immunodeficiency, which feature is MOST concerning in this patient?
questions.exp: The SPUR mnemonic stands for Serious, Persistent, Unusual, and Recurrent infections. Infection with Pneumocystis jirovecii represents an 'Unusual' pathogen that typically affects immunocompromised individuals, making this the most alarming warning sign for primary immunodeficiency.

questions.q: In the Ridley-Jopling classification, a patient with Subpolar Lepromatous leprosy (LLs) can be differentiated from Polar Lepromatous leprosy (LLp) by the presence of:
opts: Asymmetrical thickened nerves with remnant borderline lesions
Higher cell-mediated immunity than borderline tuberculoid
questions.exp: Subpolar LL (LLs) develops when a borderline patient downgrades toward the lepromatous pole, retaining features such as asymmetrical nerve thickening and remnant borderline skin lesions. Polar LL (LLp) represents the true anergic pole with diffuse, symmetrical involvement from the onset.

questions.q: A 35-year-old HIV-positive man presents with violaceous nodules on his palate and lower extremities. Biopsy confirms Kaposi sarcoma. Which virus is etiologically responsible for this malignancy?
questions.exp: Kaposi sarcoma is a lymphoangioproliferative tumor caused by Human Herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8). EBV is associated with primary CNS lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, while HPV drives cervical and anal carcinomas in HIV patients.

questions.q: A 28-year-old HIV-positive woman has a CD4 count of 80 cells/μL and positive Toxoplasma IgG serology. Which prophylactic regimen is most appropriate to prevent Toxoplasma encephalitis?
questions.exp: TMP-SMX is the preferred primary prophylaxis for Toxoplasma gondii encephalitis in HIV-positive patients with CD4 <100 cells/μL who are Toxoplasma IgG seropositive. This regimen also provides protection against Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with a linear band of sclerotic skin extending from the forehead to the scalp with underlying atrophy. His mother is concerned about joint involvement. Which statement regarding linear morphea is correct?
opts: It shows a strong female predominance similar to plaque morphea
It is the most common subtype of morphea overall
It primarily affects the trunk bilaterally
questions.exp: Linear morphea characteristically follows Blaschko's lines and commonly affects the limbs, face, frontoparietal region, and scalp. Unlike other morphea subtypes, linear morphea shows no gender preference and can cause significant morbidity when crossing joints, leading to contractures.

questions.q: A 58-year-old man presents with well-demarcated, erythematous patches on his buttocks and trunk that have been present for several years without spreading to other sites. Skin biopsy reveals atypical lymphocytes with cerebriform nuclei in the epidermis. The neoplastic cells are CD3+, CD4+, CD45RO+, and CD8-. Which of the following best explains the localized, fixed nature of this patient's cutaneous lesions?
opts: Derivation from Central Memory T-cells expressing CCR7 and L-selectin
Derivation from non-recirculating Tissue-Resident Memory T-cells
Loss of Cutaneous Lymphocyte Antigen expression
Constitutive activation of NF-κB signaling pathway
questions.exp: Mycosis fungoides is derived from non-recirculating Tissue-Resident Memory T-cells (TRM), which explains the characteristic presentation of fixed, localized patches and plaques in the skin. In contrast, Sézary syndrome derives from Central Memory T-cells (TCM) that recirculate, causing generalized erythroderma.

questions.q: During HSV latency in sensory ganglia, the viral genome exists in a specific molecular configuration and expresses limited gene products. What is the form of the viral genome during latency and what is primarily transcribed?
opts: Circular plasmid; viral DNA polymerase genes
questions.exp: During HSV latency, the viral genome circularizes into an extrachromosomal episome within the neuronal nucleus. The virus ceases active replication and expresses only Latency-Associated Transcripts (LATs), which are unique non-coding RNAs.

questions.q: Which of the following clinical features best differentiates urticarial vasculitis from ordinary chronic urticaria?
opts: Duration of individual lesions less than 24 hours
Residual purpura or hyperpigmentation after lesion resolution
questions.exp: In urticarial vasculitis, individual wheals persist for more than 24 hours and resolve with residual changes such as purpura, hyperpigmentation, or ecchymosis due to underlying leukocytoclastic vasculitis with vessel wall damage. Ordinary urticaria lesions resolve completely within 24 hours without sequelae.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with flaccid blisters predominantly affecting the trunk and oral mucosa. Direct immunofluorescence shows intercellular IgG deposits in a 'fishnet' pattern, with antibodies targeting a 130 kD glycoprotein. Which desmosomal component is most likely targeted?
questions.exp: Desmoglein 3 (Dsg3) is a 130 kD glycoprotein predominantly expressed in basal keratinocytes and oral mucosa, making it the target in pemphigus vulgaris. Dsg1 is 160 kD and more expressed in upper epidermis, while Dsg3 involvement explains the mucosal predominance.

questions.q: A 42-year-old woman presents with recurrent urticarial lesions that persist for more than 36 hours and resolve with residual hyperpigmentation. Laboratory investigations reveal low C1q, C3, and C4 levels along with positive anti-C1q antibodies. She also has arthralgia and episodic episcleritis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: This patient meets the major criteria for HUVS (urticaria >6 months and hypocomplementemia) along with minor criteria including vasculitis pattern, arthralgia, and episcleritis. The presence of anti-C1q antibodies with low C1q levels is characteristic of this condition, also known as McDuffie syndrome.

questions.q: A 28-year-old pregnant woman with untreated secondary syphilis delivers a stillborn infant at 32 weeks gestation. What is the approximate probability of transplacental transmission of Treponema pallidum during primary or secondary syphilis?
questions.exp: The probability of transmission to the fetus is highest when the mother has early syphilis (primary or secondary stages) due to high concentrations of treponemes in the blood, ranging from 70% to 100%. This produces a severe effect on the fetus.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with her first episode of painful genital ulcers. Type-specific serological testing is ordered to differentiate between HSV-1 and HSV-2. Which viral glycoprotein provides the antigenic basis for this type-specific serological distinction?
questions.exp: Glycoprotein G (gG) is antigenically type-specific, with gG-1 identifying HSV-1 and gG-2 identifying HSV-2. This provides the basis for accurate type-specific serological testing to differentiate between the two HSV types.
